news.title: The Next Big Clean Energy Bet Borrows Its Drilling Tech From Big Oil - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
news.summary: The artificial intelligence boom is putting unprecedented pressure on global energy grids. The energy needs of planned data centers outstrip planned energy additions in many places where hyperscalers are developing massive campuses. As a result, the private and public sector alike are increasingly and urgently adopting an all-of-the-above approach to energy development, increasing the scale and lifespan of fossil fuels and renewable energies alike, while also pouring funding into the research and development of next-gen energy alternatives. One of those promising energy alternatives is enhanced geothermal. Geothermal energy itself is nothing new about 85 percent of all houses in Iceland have been heated with geothermal energy for years now. But that kind of geothermal energy is only viable in geologically anomalous places like Iceland, where the heat from the Earth's core naturally breaks through to the surface in the form of hot springs, geysers, or other forms of heat vents. But the emerging field of enhanced geothermal seeks to make geothermal energy viable anywhere on Earth by digging deep enough to access that heat and pump it to the surface. In order to do that, geothermal startups and research projects are borrowing technology from a sector that knows a whole lot about drilling Big Oil. That's right, the next big thing in clean and green energy may come in the form of none other than fracking. Hydraulic fracturing could allow geothermal initiatives to cost-effectively drill to extreme depths where thermal heat is naturally abundant in order to provide a source of zero-emissions energy 24 hours a day, seven days a week. "If you drill down deep enough three, four, even six kilometers you reach the point where the crust is uniformly hot," University of California Irvine engineer Mohammad Javad Abdolhosseini Qomi was quoted in a recent article from the UC Newsroom. "Then you can drill horizontally, create fractures, and pipe in water." The rock heats the water, turning it to steam that can run turbines that generate electricity. However, we still have a long way to go before that can be achieved at a commercially viable scale. "There is more than enough potential geothermal energy underground to power the entire United States, but unlocking it safely and economically is still a major challenge," Qomi went on to say. Scientists at the University of California are one of many groups trying to find a pathway toward bringing enhanced geothermal out of lab-based modeling and into the market. Some private companies are likewise working on employing hydraulic fracturing technology to unlock commercial enhanced geothermal. Meanwhile, others are employing techniques from the field of nuclear fusion, using a vacuum-tube gyrotron to vaporize rock molecules with high-frequency electromagnetic waves down a borehole. The round-the-clock energy potential of enhanced geothermal is just one of the sector's benefits. Another critical advantage of the sector is its broad, bipartisan appeal as one of the vanishingly few forms of clean energy to receive equally enthusiastic policy support under the Biden and Trump administrations. The UC project is backed by the U.S. Department of Energy's Genesis Mission as part of this push. The Department of Energy is bullish about the potential of geothermal in the future of the United States' energy mix. Projections from the agency state that enhanced geothermal projects could provide about 90 gigawatts of carbon-free energy in the U.S. by 2050, or approximately enough to power at least 65 million homes. Big Tech is also throwing its weight behind enhanced geothermal research and development. Quaise Energy, a startup employing the fusion-derived gyrotron approach, just signed a major power purchase agreement with Google to supply 50 megawatts MW of superhot geothermal power, beginning as soon as 2030. The deal stands as a major vote of confidence in the nascent sector. By Haley Zaremba for Oilprice.com

news.title: Something Strange Just Happened in the Ukraine War: Russia, with Its Vast Crude Oil, Is Importing Fuel and Rationing Gasoline and Diesel - National Security Journal
news.summary: Ukraine launched further large-scale drone attacks on Russian infrastructure overnight Wednesday into Thursday, hitting an oil pumping station in Bashkortostan and reportedly attacking a key power plant. Russia’s Defense Ministry claimed that its air defense systems had intercepted and destroyed 343 Ukrainian drones overnight, according to state news agency TASS. Tu-22M3 Bomber from Russia. Image Credit: Creative Commons. The attacks followed a threat from Russian President Vladimir Putin on Tuesday to respond to Kyiv’s escalating attacks on Russia’s oil sector. Ukraine Says it Hit Oil Supply Center The Ukrainian General Staff confirmed on Thursday that its armed forces had attacked the Subkhankulovo oil supply and pumping center in Bashkortostan–part of Russian state-owned oil pipeline company Transneft. “Each such hit means less oil for refining and fewer oil rubles for which Russia is waging war,” the General Staff said in a Telegram statement, as quoted by The Kyiv Independent. Bulat Musin, head of the Tuymazinsky district administration, said drone debris had fallen in the industrial area and started a fire, according to local Russian news outlet Bashinform. No casualties have been reported. Independent Russian news website Astra was able to pinpoint the target based on video footage provided by witnesses. “The extent of the damage is still being assessed,” the Ukrainian open-source intelligence monitoring channel Exilenova+ said in a Thursday social media post. On Thursday, Ukraine’s General Staff reported that an oil storage tank had been hit and that a fire had broken out at the facility. While the center had been targeted in July, there was no immediate information that oil flow at the center had been disrupted. T-90M. Image Credit: Creative Commons. Second Samara Refinery Ablaze Further video footage apparently showed a fire at the Kuibyshev oil refinery in Samara, owned by the Russian state-controlled oil company Rosneft. Ukraine’s military said on Wednesday that it had targeted and damaged both the Kuibyshev and Syzran oil refineries. It said it had hit oil refining and storage units. Each refinery had already undergone about two months of repairs after Ukrainian attacks in September, the Ukrainian Defense Ministry said. It was not immediately clear whether Thursday’s fire was caused by another attack, Hromadske said. Nevinnomyssk Power Plant Likely Targeted Stavropol Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said on Thursday on Telegram that “the industrial zone of Nevinnomyssk” had been subjected to a “massive drone attack.” Falling debris had fallen near “industrial and energy facilities,” according to The Kyiv Independent’s English translation of the governor’s post. Two people were taken to a medical facility. The governor also said that educational institutions had been damaged. Astra concluded that the Nevinnomyssk thermal power plant was likely to have been the target, based on analysis of video. The plant provides power for local industry, including a large chemical firm owned by the EuroChem group. Ukrainian officials have previously referred to the chemical firm as “a critical component” of Russia’s defense production sector. Tu-95 Bomber from Russia. Image Credit: Creative Commons. Kyiv has not claimed responsibility for the Nevinnomyssk attack. Russian Oil Refining in Crisis Russian oil refining activity has plummeted to its lowest level for over 20 years, Bloomberg has said. Russian oil refineries were operating at between 2.6 million and 2.7 million barrels per day-roughly half the output seen on October 30, said Viktor Kurilov, senior oil analyst at Rystad Energy. However, these data did not include Wednesday’s attacks on Samara’s refineries. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak acknowledged on Wednesday that Russia’s domestic fuel market was “quite tense.” Putin acknowledged during a Kremlin meeting on Russia’s fuel and energy sector on Tuesday that the market for oil products “remains challenging.” In addition, several Russian regions have introduced controls on the sale of gasoline and diesel, and Moscow has had to import oil products as, despite Russia’s vast crude oil resources, the domestic market is struggling. Ukraine’s Defense Ministry said in an analysis on November 15 that its actions were exerting “sustained pressure on an entire production and logistics chain.” Moscow Braces Itself for Winter Drone Attacks Russia’s Deputy Prime Minister Marat Khusnullin told legislators on Wednesday that ensuring Russia’s energy infrastructure survived the winter was a top state concern. Tu-95. Image Credit: Creative Commons. “This is now the most important question: how we’ll get through the winter, especially given drone attacks,” Khusnullin was quoted by Reuters as saying. His statement was made as Russia itself was continuing with its large-scale attacks on Ukrainian civilian energy infrastructure. At a meeting at the Kremlin on Tuesday, Putin said: “Retaliatory measures on our part are inevitable.” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha hit back at Putin’s remarks via X on Tuesday. “If Putin doesn’t like Ukraine’s strikes on his oil refineries, he can order an end to the war,” Sybiha said, adding: “Stop complaining. End the war.” About the Author: Georgia Gilholy Georgia Gilholy is a journalist based in the United Kingdom who has been published in Newsweek, The Times of Israel, and the Spectator. Gilholy writes about international politics, culture, and education.

news.title: WiseTech Faces Market Pressure as Oil Prices Lift Energy Stocks - www.suaralandak.co.id
news.summary: Rising oil prices and geopolitical uncertainty in the Middle East are reshaping investor sentiment across Australia's share market, creating contrasting conditions for energy and technology companies. WiseTech Global Ltd (ASX:WTC), a major logistics software provider, is among the technology stocks attracting attention as investors reassess sector exposure and operating costs. Market data recorded WiseTech shares at AUD 54.46, up AUD 7.650 or 16.343%, at 23:55 UTC on November 26, 2026.The company's position within the ASX 200 also makes its performance relevant to broader assessments of Australia's listed technology sector. The latest market environment reflects competing pressures. Higher crude oil prices have supported energy stocks following escalating tensions in the Middle East, while rising commodity costs and changing investor risk appetite have created challenges for growth-oriented technology shares, according to the market analysis published by Kalkine Media.WiseTech operates in the supply chain technology industry, providing software that supports freight forwarding and customs operations across international markets. Its flagship platform helps logistics operators manage shipping documentation, regulatory compliance, freight rates and shipment tracking.These services support the administrative processes behind international cargo movements. Businesses use the software to coordinate complex logistics activities, making technology an important component of freight operations. Disruptions across global shipping routes have also increased operational complexity for logistics companies. Port congestion, changing trade routes, shipping diversions and tighter customs requirements have created additional administrative demands across the freight industry.Geopolitical tensions can intensify these challenges when maritime operators need to avoid strategically sensitive shipping routes. Longer transit times and changes to transportation arrangements can increase documentation and coordination requirements. Higher oil prices present a separate challenge for the logistics industry because fuel expenses contribute to transportation costs. At the same time, the market analysis highlights how greater operational complexity can increase the importance of automation and logistics management software.For technology investors, the distinction between company performance and broader market movements remains relevant. Changes in sector valuations can reflect shifts in capital allocation and investor sentiment rather than developments within an individual company's operations. Energy companies have benefited from the latest movement in crude prices.Woodside Energy Group Ltd (ASX:WDS), one of Australia's major listed oil and gas producers, is among the companies closely watched when international oil markets experience significant movements. Higher energy costs can also influence freight expenses, business input costs and the valuation of companies whose expected earnings extend further into the future. These factors can weigh on technology shares even when their underlying business operations have not experienced an equivalent change.The market session also featured developments in Australia's banking sector. Bank of Queensland Ltd (ASX:BOQ) reported lower cash earnings year on year alongside higher revenue during its fiscal first half, according to the source report.The combination highlights different pressures facing regional lenders, including funding expenses, margin conditions and investment in business transformation. Revenue growth and cash earnings therefore presented contrasting indicators of the bank's financial performance. Banking developments also provide context for Australia's broader financial sector, where technology investment remains relevant to operational efficiency and digital infrastructure.Financial institutions are significant users of enterprise software as they continue to manage their technology requirements. Australia's share market remains heavily represented by financial services and resources companies, although internationally focused software businesses have gradually increased their presence. WiseTech's position within the ASX 200 reflects the growing importance of technology companies in the domestic equity market.

news.title: Oil prices fall amid forecasts of global oversupply - Inspenet
news.summary:
The oil prices retreated on Wednesday, November 25, amid expectations of a global crude oil surplus, forecasts of supply exceeding demand weighed more heavily on prices than fears of potential supply disruptions in the Middle East.

The Brent crude futures they fell 0.5% to $90.96 per barrel, while the West Texas Intermediate (WTI) it registered a drop of 0.8%, to $81.43 per barrel, according to quotes at 10:35 GMT.

This pullback comes after both oil benchmarks registered gains of more than 2% during the previous session.

The forecasts of the International Energy Agency (IEA) they point to a global crude oil surplus, a scenario that is keeping prices under pressure. This is compounded by the increase in oil inventories in the United States.

According to data from American Petroleum Institute (API) , US crude oil inventories increased by 126,000 barrels during the week ending November 20.

Furthermore, the reactivation of the Sharara oil pipeline in Libya allowed the resumption of crude oil transport to the Akakus storage facilities in Zawiya.

Oil market operators are also keeping a close eye on the meetings of the OPEC+ scheduled for November 29, in which the ministers will address the crude oil production policy for 2027.

Ahead of these meetings, Iraq is seeking an upward revision of the alliance’s estimate of its extraction capacity. This revision will be crucial in determining member countries’ production quotas for the coming year.

Despite the prospects of oversupply, the situation in the Middle East continues to generate uncertainty among energy market participants.

The Houthis in Yemen claimed to have attacked the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia, a facility that is part of a strategic complex for processing and exporting Saudi oil.

Added to this situation are the recent maritime incidents in the Strait of Hormuz, which maintain concerns about the safety of international hydrocarbon transport.

For now, expectations of a global crude oil surplus outweigh geopolitical risks and are keeping oil prices down throughout the day.

news.title: Standard Chartered Oil Needs a New Shock to Fall Further - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
news.summary: Oil prices continued to recover from their recent slump, with renewed Middle East supply threats outweighing earlier global surplus concerns. Brent crude for January delivery climbed 1.3% to trade at $95.90 per barrel at 12.00 pm ET on Thursday, a sharp rise after closing at $89.37/bbl on Monday while the corresponding WTI crude contract was up 1.2% to change hands at $84.65/ bbl. Yemen's Houthi forces claimed on Wednesday that their strikes on Saudi Arabia's Ras Tanura oil refinery and export complex caused fires, with satellite imagery from NASA and Planet Labs revealing thick black smoke over the site. The Houthis also claimed multiple strikes on Riyadh's financial district, where Saudi civil defense reported 11 people were injured on Tuesday after a strike hit a tower housing the Public Investment Fund for the second time in under a week. U.S. commercial crude oil inventories rose by 1.1 million barrels to 418.9 million barrels in the week ended November 20, marking a third consecutive weekly build as higher net imports and domestic output outweighed increased refinery runs while crude exports dropped to their lowest level since early August amid higher freight costs and softer Asian demand. Traders will be watching the November 29 OPEC ministerial meeting, where members are set to discuss 2027 production policy amid competing views on potential supply surpluses and internal quota disputes. And now, oil and commodity experts at Standard Chartered have weighed in, saying that oil prices are unlikely to sink below recent lows, with further downside needing clearer evidence of sustained inventory builds or a faster recovery in physical supply, even as the geopolitical uncertainty continues to complicate the outlook. Brent crude spent much of the past week consolidating around the low $90s/bbl, following a sharp correction from the late-October highs, before slipping below $90/bbl on Monday with the $89.37/bbl settlement the lowest in nearly three months. Related Goldman Sachs Sees U.S. Natural Gas Demand Surging on Data Center Boom According to the analysts, the price action reflects the increasingly entrenched bearish fundamental narrative, which was reinforced by the IEA's substantial upward revision to Q4 supply. The IEA raised its Q4 supply estimate by 3.3mb/d in its November Oil Market Report, reflecting a faster recovery in Gulf production and exports than previously expected. This has reinforced expectations of a return to surplus by the end of the year, coupled with a more substantial build in 2027. However, StanChart says that the recent price correction has already discounted much of the anticipated supply surplus, implying that a sustained move lower may require evidence that the surplus will emerge sooner, be larger, or persist for longer than currently expected, rather than simply confirming existing forecasts. That said, there's an ongoing broad decline across refined product prices, refining margins and freight rates, suggesting that some of the exceptional tightness associated with geopolitical disruptions is beginning to unwind. According to StanChart, European jet fuel NWE Jet CIF cargo balance of month and Asian fuel oil Singapore 380 M1 prices declined 24% and 31% MTD, respectively, while the European diesel crack ICE gasoil/Brent spread has fallen 21%, indicating that the adjustment extends beyond falling crude prices. Refining economics have also weakened, with both Asian FCC margins and NWE hydrocracking margins down 25% MTD. Meanwhile, Middle East-to-China TD3C clean product freight rates have declined 27%, while dirty VLCC freight rates on the Gulf-to-China route have fallen 55% MTD. These developments provide increasingly broad evidence of easing market stress, although absolute prices and transportation costs remain elevated. However, the gradual easing of physical market tightness continues against a backdrop of uncertain diplomatic progress between Washington and Tehran, with the latest spate of attacks on regional energy infrastructure and shipping underscoring the vulnerability of the physical supply recovery. The muted price response suggests that the market is increasingly discounting persistent hostilities in the absence of material additional supply losses. StanChart has predicted that a diplomatic breakthrough could accelerate the resumption of physical flows and reinforce downward price pressure, while renewed disruptions to export infrastructure or maritime routes could quickly challenge expectations of a surplus. Continued attacks on Russian energy infrastructure also constrain the recovery in middle distillate availability, even as broader crude supply conditions improve. Meanwhile, OPEC meets on Sunday, three months after it completed the rollback of 1.65 million bpd of voluntary cuts with a final 188,000 bpd increase in September. The group then agreed to hold September targets through December, according to Rystad Energy. StanChart says members now have to decide whether to add barrels, hold steady or cut again as surplus forecasts grow. They also have to settle their 2027 production baselines without splitting the group. Iraq's weight in the group grew when the UAE left in May, "although not necessarily its formal influence," the bank says. Baghdad has a long record of producing above its quota and wants OPEC to recognize its higher production capacity. Recent OPEC meetings have barely moved prices. StanChart says Sunday's could, particularly if members agree to act together on supply again. The analysts note that the UAE's departure in May has increased the relative importance of Iraq, although not necessarily its formal influence. Iraq has historically been among the group's least compliant members on quotas and is seeking recognition of its higher production capacity. StanChart says that whereas recent OPEC meetings have elicited little market reaction, the Sunday meeting could prove more consequential for near-term crude prices, particularly if it signals a renewed and collective willingness to manage supply in response to an increasingly bearish balance. By Alex Kimani for Oilprice.com

news.summary: Brazil Defies Trump Tariffs as China Slams US Measures - Islam Times 0 Friday 27 November 2026 - 02:55 Brazil Defies Trump Tariffs as China Slams US Measures Story Code : 1314223 The new tariffs target 14 major trading partners and have triggered objections from several governments. Brazil's government described Washington's unilateral decision as "unacceptable," particularly criticizing proposed higher import duties on raw and refined sugar and a new 10% tariff on aircraft, which would affect Brazilian manufacturer Embraer. Brasilia said it would continue negotiations while keeping retaliatory measures on the table in response to what it described as the illegal imposition of tariffs on its products. China faces some of the highest proposed duties, with US tariff rates potentially reaching 20% and, in certain cases, combining with existing levies to reach 45%. A Chinese embassy spokesperson rejected Washington's allegations of industrial overcapacity, warning against using the issue as a pretext for political manipulation. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun also stressed that neither a tariff war nor a trade war serves any country's interests, calling for dialogue and implementation of existing agreements between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. The European Union also rejected the proposed measures, urging Washington to honor its existing trade agreement. Vietnam, India and Taiwan expressed concerns over the findings, while Japan and Singapore criticized the proposed tariffs. Other affected economies include South Korea, Indonesia, Malaysia, Thailand, Bangladesh, Cambodia and Switzerland. The US administration said the proposed duties would be capped at lower rates under existing or ongoing trade agreements, with public hearings and industry consultations scheduled before implementation, potentially in February or March. The latest measures have also drawn criticism within the United States. Democratic Senator Ron Wyden condemned Trump's tariff policy as an attempt to impose unilateral global duties, pledging to use available legislative tools to challenge the measures. Meanwhile, US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer defended the tariffs, arguing that trading partners' practices had undermined American manufacturing and distorted global trade balances. news.summary: Gold prices recovered as investors returned to precious metals following a sharp sell-off earlier in the week, although mounting expectations of further US interest rate increases continue to cloud the outlook. Spot gold climbed 1.70% to US$3,627.43 an ounce, while silver outperformed with a gain of 4.98%. Platinum advanced 3.01% and palladium rose 2.72%. The recovery follows a volatile period for bullion, which briefly dropped below US$3,500 on Wednesday and remains under pressure after suffering a 9.4% decline last week, its steepest weekly loss in eight months. Gold has traded below US$4,000 an ounce since November 11 and remains on course for a third monthly decline exceeding 6%. Inflation strengthens case for US rate hikes The latest US inflation figures have complicated gold's recovery prospects, strengthening expectations that the Federal Reserve will tighten monetary policy further. Core personal consumption expenditures inflation, the Fed's preferred measure of underlying price pressures, accelerated to 3.3% in October, its highest annual reading since 2023. Interest rate futures are now pricing in a 96.2% probability of a 25-basis-point increase at the Fed's December 9 meeting. Markets also assign a 64.3% probability that the federal funds rate will reach a target range of 4.25% to 4.50% by the January 27 meeting. Higher interest rates generally work against gold by increasing the opportunity cost of holding an asset that generates no income. Rising energy costs stemming from Middle East tensions have added to inflationary pressures, weakening expectations of monetary policy relief heading into 2027. Precious metals join broader market recovery Gold's rebound coincided with gains across European and Asian equity markets on Thursday, as investors returned to technology stocks following recent heavy selling. US equity markets remained closed for Thanksgiving, limiting trading activity and potentially contributing to volatility across commodity markets. Silver's stronger recovery points to renewed buying across metals with industrial applications, although concerns about global economic growth remain. Australian gold miners face uncertain outlook For Australian gold producers, the recovery offers some relief after several weeks of falling bullion prices and heightened share market volatility. However, rising diesel, labour and financing costs could squeeze operating margins if gold prices remain subdued. A weaker Australian dollar could provide some protection for domestic producers by supporting local currency gold prices. With US inflation proving stubborn and financial markets increasingly anticipating successive interest rate increases, gold's latest rebound faces a difficult test before investors can declare an end to the recent sell-off.

Wall Street was closed on Nov 26 for the Thanksgiving holiday, but in Asia, S&P 500 futures were up 0.8% and Nasdaq futures were 1% higher.

Japan’s Nikkei rose 0.7% to bring its gains for the week to 2.7%, clawing back only a fraction of its 8.4% loss for November .

Data showed on Nov 27 that core inflation in Tokyo hit a 16-month high in November, bolstering the case for an interest rate hike from the Bank of Japan as soon as December .

MSCI’s broadest index of Asia-Pacific shares outside Japan edged up 0.5% to end the week 1.9% higher. It was still down 8.2% for November .

Shares in South Korea rallied 2% and China’s blue chips slipped 0.2%, after hitting the lowest level since June 2025 on Nov 26 .

“Barring a big shock that severely rattles a thin market, November is practically in the books and the markets limp into December where a seasonal ‘Santa Rally’ currently appears elusive,” said Kyle Rodda, a senior analyst at Capital. com

“For as long as the markets remain unsure about the growth trajectory for AI and lack clarity about where US rates may peak, uncertainty and therefore volatility is liable to remain elevated.”

“The Fed could, of course, still blink,” said David Rees, chief economist at Schroders. “But a Fed put would not necessarily be unambiguously positive for markets.”

“If growth and inflation data remain firm, in a game of cat and mouse markets could soon begin pricing a more hawkish Fed back in, potentially setting off the same chain of events all over again.”

news.title: (BOJ Review) Developments in JGB Market-Making Business by Securities Companies
news.summary:
November 27, 2026 ASAMATSU Hiroki, AIDA Eri * , HORIKAWA Takumi, OGAWA Yoshiya Financial System and Bank Examination Department

* Previously at the Financial System and Bank Examination Department

Securities companies function as market makers in the Japanese government bond (JGB) market by intermediating the trading needs of investors. They manage the interest rate risk they bear and earn profits from their intermediation. In this paper we analyze the developments in factors that are internally considered by securities companies, such as balance sheet size, interest rate risk, and profits, as they undertake the role of market makers, and we examine the impact of these factors on liquidity in the government bond market, including through case studies. Generally, under stable market conditions, the risk management factors of securities companies rarely have a significant impact on the liquidity of the government bond market. However, during the market turmoil in April 2025, the cautious stance of securities companies toward taking on additional risks may have contributed to the widening of bid-ask spreads. Moving forward, it remains important to deepen our understanding of the developments in market-making business.

news.title: What are tariffs, how do they work and why is Trump using them? - BBC
news.summary:
Tariffs have been one of US President Donald Trump's favourite economic tools since he returned to the White House.

He argues these import taxes boost US manufacturing and create jobs. But critics say they have put up prices for American consumers and disrupted and damaged the global economy.

Tariffs are taxes on imported goods.

Typically, the charge is a percentage of a good's value.

For example, a 10% tariff on a $10 product would mean a $1 tax on top - taking the total cost to $11.

The tax is paid to the government by companies bringing in the foreign products.

These firms may pass some or all of the extra cost on to their customers, which in this case means American consumers and other US businesses.

Companies may also decide to import fewer goods.

Trump argues tariffs increase the amount of tax raised by the government, encourage consumers to buy American-made goods and boost investment in the US from foreign companies.

Parts of the US were hollowed out economically when free trade deals resulted in industrial jobs heading overseas.

Trump also wants to reduce the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

The president argues that countries that sell more products to the US than they buy from it are cheating the US and that tariffs correct this imbalance.

In February 2026, the US Supreme Court said that Trump had exceeded his authority when he used emergency powers to introduce tariffs on specific countries without approval from Congress.

That ruling affected all tariffs Trump brought in under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA).

That includes the first tariffs Trump announced in early 2025 which targeted Mexico, Canada and China.

The ruling also covers those announced on Trump's so-called "Liberation Day" in April 2025, when the president set out tariff rates of up to 50% for dozens countries, including Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia.

About $100bn (£74bn) has since been refunded to companies that paid those "Liberation Day" tariffs.

This represents roughly 60% of the roughly $166bn collected under the government policy, according to a court filing.

Around $29bn in potential refunds are still being reviewed by trade authorities, while a further $1.6bn remains unpaid because importers have not provided the banking details needed to process payments.

No. The White House has been looking at alternative ways.

After the Supreme Court ruling, Trump used different legislation - Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974 - to impose temporary 10% tariffs on all global imports.

Those tariffs expired on 24 July, but have been replaced by tariffs of 10% to 12.5% on all goods from the top 60 US trade partners, including the UK, the EU and China.

In late November, Trump announced new duties against 14 partners, including China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, which follows other similar moves made in the wake of the SCOTUS ruling against the administration.

The actions have been taken under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices.

The Trump administration has begun arguing that the tariffs target what it calls "overcapacity" or that some countries are making more goods than they need and then selling them cheaply in the US, which makes it difficult for American companies to compete.

Over the summer, 25 US states - all Democrat-controlled - launched legal action that calls these tariffs "arbitrary, capricious, and contrary to law". The lawsuit accuses the administration of using forced labour as a pretext to continue tariffs.

Trump also used Section 301 to levy a 25% tax on certain goods from Brazil, claiming that Brazilian policies have harmed US trade.

In August, he announced a 50% tariff on a wide range of goods imported from Canada, in retaliation for what he called "unequal treatment" of US cars, dairy and alcohol, under Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930.

Those tariffs cover about $20bn (C$28bn; £14bn) of Canadian imports, or about 5% of all goods Canada sends south.

The UK had already negotiated a 10% tariff with the US on most goods in June 2025.

The latest announcement does not change that, but tariffs have been removed on whisky imports, something Trump had said he would do after the King's state visit to the US earlier this year .

In 2024, the UK exported about £58bn of goods to the US - mainly cars, machinery and pharmaceuticals.

Under the terms of the 2025 deal, the 10% rate applied to the first 100,000 UK vehicles exported every year - roughly the number sold in 2024. Additional cars face the standard 25% tariff.

UK steel exports to the US are also subject to 25% duty, compared to the 50% rate which applies to steel and aluminium products from the rest of the world.

Many firms said they would pass on the cost of tariffs to US customers, including Target, Walmart and Adidas.

Some products have become more expensive - including toys, appliances and furniture as well as certain foodstuffs.

The cost of some goods manufactured in the US using imported components has also gone up.

In October 2025, a study by Goldman Sachs estimated that about 55% of the tariff charges were passed on to US consumers.

And in April, a Federal Reserve study said Trump's sweeping 2025 tariffs had caused a surge in inflation this year.

The White House has always maintained that it will take time for the tariffs to pay off, pointing to promises by firms and countries to make big investments in the US.

Despite the new barriers to trade, US imports actually increased by 4% in 2025.

Trump was accused of throwing the global economy into turmoil when he announced the first tariffs of his second presidential term in early 2025.

Share prices around the world fell sharply, as did the value of the dollar.

Although the US currency and global financial markets have since largely recovered, the ongoing uncertainty around Trump's tariff policy has continued to destabilise international trade.

Some US allies have looked to alternative markets, causing what some economists describe as a "re-wiring" of global trade.

In January 2026, the International Monetary Fund (IMF) said the tariffs had "definitely [slowed] down global activity", and warned further trade tensions could threaten economic growth.

Since then the Iran war has restricted the global supply of oil and fertiliser, pushing up prices.

news.title: Oil Prices Climb as Middle East Supply Risks Overshadow Glut Fears - Crude Oil Prices Today | OilPrice.com
news.summary: Crude oil prices were set to book a weekly gain after a string of losses, as increasingly frequent reports about tanker attacks in the Strait of Hormuz undermined expectations of a glut. Data showing lower than pre-war levels of energy commodity exports from the Middle East also contributed, as did the latest Houthi attacks on Saudi energy targets. At the time of writing, Brent crude was trading at $96.61 per barrel, and West Texas Intermediate was changing hands for $85.79 per barrel. Both are still down from heights reached in October but are regaining ground from their latest slump. According to some analysts, if the situation in the Middle East escalates further, Brent could rebound above $100 per barrel. “We think Brent can still push above USD100/bbl without another major escalation in the Middle East, but that increasingly requires evidence of constrained deliverable supply,” ANZ commodity analysts said this week, as quoted by Reuters. “Recent attacks on Saudi infrastructure, including areas around the key Ras Tanura export hub and Red Sea ports, alongside reports of vessels being targeted in the Strait of Hormuz, have brought supply risks back into focus,” ING analysts wrote in a note Thursday, noting that traders will also be watching the OPEC meeting this weekend to see where the group is heading with its production strategy. To be fair, supply has been in focus for months now, but in recent weeks, expectations of a glut took over the oil market coverage as the International Energy Agency assumed the September rebound in export rates would hold despite the absence of a peace deal between the United States and Iran, and any sign of willingness for compromise on either side. Now, data is showing that the IEA’s assumption has been wrong—oil flows are down from September and October highs, and LNG export rates are still half of what they used to be before the war started. news.title: Navy Uncovers Suspected Stolen Crude Oil, Illegal Refinery In Rivers - New National Star
news.summary:
By Joy Onu

The Nigerian Navy has uncovered 112,525 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and illegally refined petroleum products at four illegal refining sites in Rivers State.

According to a statement issued by the Director of Naval Information, Navy Captain Abiodun Folorunsho, the discoveries were made on November 25 during separate operations in Ogbogolo Community, Ahoada West Local Government Area, and George Pepple Community, Bonny Local Government Area, as part of the Navy’s sustained efforts to combat crude oil theft, illegal bunkering and related criminal activities.

At Ogbogolo, personnel of Nigerian Navy Ship (NNS) SOROH identified two illegal refining sites containing approximately 15,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil and 525 litres of suspected illegally refined Automotive Gas Oil (AGO). The sites also contained three cooking drum ovens, two dugout pits and other equipment used for illegal refining.

In George Pepple Community, personnel of Forward Operating Base (FOB) BONNY identified two additional refining sites with 13 dugout pits. Seven of the pits held approximately 97,000 litres of suspected stolen crude oil, while four contained water and two were freshly excavated. The Nigerian Navy said the facilities and petroleum products found during the operations were handled in accordance with established procedures.

The findings indicate continued attempts by oil thieves to establish new locations and resume illegal refining activities despite previous disruptions. It said the operations would focus on protecting critical oil and gas infrastructure, safeguarding the country’s energy resources and preventing activities that undermine the national economy.
